review.dimension: PERFORMANCE: speed, load/startup times, query optimisation
review.summary: The biggest measured costs come from avoidable repeated work, not from SQLite configuration. First, every CLI invocation rebuilds the Typer tree from string annotations: 1.185 s, falling to 0.012 s once the annotations are resolved; this alone accounts for about 42% of the navigator test files' wall time. Second, the navigator MCP server re-reads and re-normalises every held Act copy on each call: 0.53-0.79 s per call cold, against 3-9 ms warm. Third, the rule tagger runs 393 full-text regex scans per document, none of which can use re's literal-prefix fast path: 1,437.6 s for the 397-document corpus, about 92% of parse CPU, against 43.8 s for redact and 75.4 s for parse_statute. Smaller wins are a normalise() that is 8x faster with identical output, a CCMA catalogue whose FTS deletes are full scans (seeding 4x the records took 25x longer), a quadratic RTF stripper, and test-only fixes for 6 s of real sleeps and roughly 2 s per default httpx client in tests. All timings were taken at 100% CPU contention from other agents, so absolute numbers are inflated; every comparison was run side by side in one process, and the equivalent rewrites were checked for identical output.
measurements: CPU load during session: 100% (Get-CimInstance Win32_Processor); bare `python -c pass` 0.19 s; `python -m labour_corpus --help` 4.5-9.3 s over 5 runs

python -X importtime -c 'import labour_corpus.cli': cumulative 5.41 s, of which pypdf 1.02 s (18.8%, via parse/pdf.py), httpx 0.58 s, typer 0.72 s; labour_corpus.navigator.mcp_server imports neither pypdf nor httpx (1.32 s)

pytest tests/test_navigator.py + tests/test_navigator_phase2.py (83 passed): 31.2 s / 26.0 s as-is vs 17.5 s / 15.1 s with a scratch plugin resolving typer annotations

Real corpus (mode=ro): 397 documents; LRA copies by title 3 (1,055,112 chars), EEA 5; CorpusSource LRA load+normalise 0.809 s

All 393 tagger patterns start with \b. Rewriting the leading `\bX` as `X(?<!\w\w)` on 98 sampled patterns over a 478,615-char text: 8.92 s to 4.16 s (2.1x) with identical match spans. Skipping a regex when no casefolded word token starts with its mandatory leading literal: 62.6 s to 35.1 s over 8 documents (1.23 s to 0.19 s on a 20 KB document), with identical TaggingResult

findings.title: Every CLI invocation spends ~1.2 s evaluating stringified Typer annotations
findings.what: cli.py:7, ccma/cli.py:14 and navigator/cli.py:8 use `from __future__ import annotations`. On every invocation, including --help, `navigate assess`, `search` and each CliRunner call in tests, Typer builds all 25 command callbacks. For each one it calls typing.get_type_hints and inspect.signature(eval_str=True), which compile and eval each string annotation (250 compile and 500 eval calls per build).
findings.why: Measured best of 4: typer.main.get_command(app) takes 1.185 s with string annotations and 0.012 s with resolved annotations (99.8x). It is paid by every command a user runs and by every CliRunner test: the navigator test files drop from 31.2 s to 17.5 s and from 26.0 s to 15.1 s, with all 83 tests passing.
findings.how: Remove `from __future__ import annotations` from the three Typer modules: cli.py, ccma/cli.py and navigator/cli.py. Every annotation type used there (Path, str, int, bool, `str | None`, `tuple[int, int] | None`, Console, CaseFacts, InMemorySource, date) is imported at module top and evaluates fine on Python 3.11 or later. Leave the import in non-CLI modules.
findings.expected_impact: About 1.17 s off every CLI invocation (99.8x on the command-tree build) and about 42% off the navigator test files (measured 26-31 s to 15-17.5 s).
findings.proving_test: Full suite passes unchanged. Add a test that `typer.main.get_command(app)` completes in under 0.2 s, or that no annotation of a registered callback is a str.

findings.title: Navigator MCP server re-reads and re-normalises every Act copy on each tool call
findings.what: NavigatorServer._assess (line 99) and _provisions (line 112) build a fresh CorpusSource for every call, so its per-instance `_cache` (grounding.py:70) is always empty. Each call reopens corpus.sqlite, reads every held LRA copy (about 1.05 M chars) and, for provisions, every EEA copy from text/, and normalises them all again.
findings.why: This is the product's interactive path. Measured per navigator_assess call in a long-lived server: 0.53-0.79 s. navigator_provisions takes 0.85-1.62 s. The same assessment with a reused warm source takes 2.8-8.7 ms, so more than 99% of each call is redundant I/O and normalisation.
findings.how: Keep one CorpusSource on the server instance and reuse it across calls. Invalidate it when the corpus changes: before each call, compare corpus_db.stat().st_mtime_ns plus `SELECT MAX(updated_at) FROM documents` (one cheap read-only query) with the values the cache was built under, and rebuild on mismatch. This preserves D-018's 'never answer from a stale corpus' and D-022's run-time re-finding: the substring check still runs every call, and only load and normalise are cached.
findings.expected_impact: Repeat navigator_assess calls drop from about 0.5-0.8 s to about 3-9 ms (more than 60x); navigator_provisions from about 0.85-1.6 s to milliseconds.
findings.proving_test: Spy on CorpusSource.texts_for loading (or count sqlite3.connect calls): two navigator_assess calls trigger one load. Touching the db mtime, or inserting a newer updated_at row in a tmp corpus, triggers a reload and the new text is grounded.

findings.title: Tagger runs 393 full-document regex scans, none able to use re's literal-prefix search
findings.what: _match_tag runs every compiled pattern over the whole text. All 393 patterns begin with `\b`, which stops sre from extracting a literal prefix, so every pattern attempts a match at every character position. Matched patterns also scan twice: search() and then finditer() from offset 0 (lines 98 and 102).
findings.why: This is the dominant parse cost. Measured: 65.9 s for one 1.08 MB text and 1,437.6 s (24 min) across all 397 corpus texts, against 43.8 s for redact and 75.4 s for parse_statute over the same set. Every `parse` re-run (as after D-024) and every CCMA seed pays it.
findings.how: Three exactly-equivalent steps, keeping the D-005 rules unchanged. (1) Drop the separate search(): record the pattern on the first finditer hit. (2) At import, rewrite a leading `\b<letter>` as `<letter>(?<!\w\w)` (390 of 393 qualify); measured 2.1x with identical spans. (3) Per document, build the sorted set of casefolded \w+ tokens and skip any pattern whose mandatory leading literal (the letters after \b, minus a trailing optional letter) prefixes no token; measured 1.8x overall and 6.5x on mid-size documents, with identical TaggingResult on 8 documents.
findings.expected_impact: Roughly 3-4x less tagging CPU (estimated from 2.1x and 1.8x measured separately, plus removing the double scan), i.e. about 24 min down to about 6-8 min for a full re-parse under the same load, with identical tags.
findings.proving_test: Golden-equality test: run the current and the optimised tag_document over every tests/fixtures text plus a sample of data/corpus/text and assert identical TaggingResult (evidence, tags, outcome, remedy, confidence); a per-pattern test asserts identical finditer spans for the rewritten patterns.

findings.title: grounding.normalise is 8x slower than an output-identical formulation
findings.what: str.translate with a dict map containing non-Latin-1 keys (U+2018/2019/201C/201D/2013/2014) takes CPython's slow per-character path; on 1.24 M chars it costs 0.40 s. The \s+ regex substitution adds another 0.20 s.
findings.why: This cost is paid by every cold grounding: each CLI `navigate assess`, the first MCP call, and the real-corpus test test_every_provision_is_verified_in_the_real_corpus (2.53 s). Measured on all 8 held Act copies: 0.725 s.
findings.how: Replace it with eight chained str.replace calls over the same pairs (each is a fast memchr-style pass), then `' '.join(text.split()).lower()`. str.split() and re's \s both use Unicode isspace, and strip() is implied. Measured 0.091 s with output identical on all 8 copies.
findings.expected_impact: 0.725 s to 0.091 s (8x) per cold load of LRA and EEA; about 0.5 s off each CLI navigate assess.
findings.proving_test: Property test comparing the old and new normalise on random strings drawn from all Unicode whitespace characters, the 8 mapped characters and ASCII letters, plus an equality check over the real held copies when present.

findings.title: Network-layer tests pay the real 1 s robots floor and about 2 s certifi SSL setup
findings.evidence:
fetcher = Fetcher("Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; test)", client=client,
                      limiter=RateLimiter(0, 0), retry_waits=(0, 0, 0))
findings.what: RobotsRules.crawl_delay() always returns at least DEFAULT_CRAWL_DELAY=1.0 (robots.py:103-107), and Fetcher passes it to RateLimiter.wait. RateLimiter(0, 0) therefore still sleeps about 1 s between attempts on a host, so the backoff test sleeps for real. Separately, test_tls.py:140 and :150 construct `Fetcher("UA")` without client=, which builds a default httpx.Client and loads certifi into an SSL context, although neither test sends a request.
findings.why: Measured: test_fetcher_backoff_schedule_retries_then_gives_up takes 6.03-6.21 s, 5.54 s of it in RateLimiter.wait (11 time.sleep calls). The two TLS tests take 3.03 s and 1.84 s; a default httpx.Client() costs 2.0-4.5 s against 0.0003 s with MockTransport. The production politeness floor is correct and must stay.
findings.how: In tests only, add `class NoWaitLimiter(RateLimiter): def wait(self, host, crawl_delay=None): return 0.0` and use it where RateLimiter(0, 0) is used (test_ccma_engine.py:199 and :478, test_ccma_official.py:575). In test_tls.py, pass `client=httpx.Client(transport=httpx.MockTransport(lambda r: httpx.Response(404)))`. Do not change DEFAULT_CRAWL_DELAY.
findings.expected_impact: About 11 s off each full-suite run (6 s backoff plus about 4.9 s TLS) out of about 75 s, roughly 14%.
findings.proving_test: The same tests pass and `pytest --durations` shows each under 0.3 s; test_robots rate-limiter tests (which use the real RateLimiter) still pass.

findings.title: CCMA catalogue FTS deletes filter on UNINDEXED columns, a full scan per upsert
findings.evidence:
c.execute(
                "DELETE FROM records_fts WHERE source=? AND native_id=?",
                (row.source, row.native_id),
findings.what: upsert_record always runs this DELETE (insert path included). FTS5 cannot index UNINDEXED columns, so EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN gives `SCAN records_fts VIRTUAL TABLE INDEX 0:` and every row's stored content is read. The same applies to `DELETE FROM knowledge_fts WHERE id=?`, which runs once per old unit at lines 347 and 360.
findings.why: Seeding is O(N²). On a scratch catalogue with 17 KB bodies, per-record seed cost rose from 18.6 ms at N=250 to 115.5 ms at N=1,000 (4x the records took 25x longer), and N=2,000 did not finish in 280 s. A re-seed update cost 217.6 ms per record against 0.011 ms for a rowid-keyed delete. The cost is latent today (1 record) but grows with any award or local_corpus volume.
findings.how: Key the FTS rows by the base table's rowid. After the records upsert, run `SELECT rowid FROM records WHERE source=? AND native_id=?` (PK index), then `DELETE FROM records_fts WHERE rowid=?` and `INSERT INTO records_fts(rowid, ...)`. Do the same for knowledge_fts against knowledge_units.rowid, switching INSERT OR REPLACE to an upsert so the rowid stays stable. Add a one-time migration that rebuilds both FTS tables with mapped rowids (or recreates records_fts from the current rows by join).
findings.expected_impact: Per-record FTS maintenance becomes O(log N): about 0.01 ms instead of 100-200 ms at N=1,000; seeding becomes linear.
findings.proving_test: Seed N=2,000 synthetic records into a tmp catalogue in under a fixed budget (for example 30 s); assert search() and get() results are identical before and after the migration; EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN of the delete shows `INDEX 0:=`.

findings.title: pypdf is imported eagerly by every CLI command, about 19% of import time
findings.evidence:
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pypdf.errors import PdfReadError
findings.what: cli.py imports pipeline, which imports parse.pdf, which imports pypdf (including its cryptography providers) at module load. ccma/extract.py:18 does the same. Commands that never read a PDF (navigate assess/interview/provisions, search, report, sources, --help) still pay for it.
findings.why: python -X importtime: pypdf cumulative 1.02 s of 5.41 s for labour_corpus.cli (18.8%); an isolated `import pypdf` takes 1.1-1.8 s against 0.19 s for a bare interpreter. The navigator MCP launcher avoids it, but the `labour-corpus navigate` CLI does not.
findings.how: Move the two pypdf imports inside extract_pdf_text (parse/pdf.py, where PdfReader is used at line 47) and into the page-count helper in ccma/extract.py (line 117), including the PdfReadError used in the except clauses. The logger-level setup at pdf.py:24 needs no import.
findings.expected_impact: About 1 s (about 19%) off import for every non-parse CLI command; no change to parse behaviour.
findings.proving_test: A test running `python -c "import labour_corpus.cli, sys; assert 'pypdf' not in sys.modules"` in a subprocess; the existing PDF tests (test_office_and_ocr.py, test_ccma_official.py paged_pdf) still pass.

findings.title: rtf_to_text copies the rest of the document for every control word, making it quadratic
findings.what: Each backslash slices raw[index:], copying the remaining string, before matching. Control-word density makes this O(n²) in document size. The function also goes through re's pattern cache on every call instead of a precompiled pattern.
findings.why: Measured on synthetic SAFLII-style RTF: 168,924 B 0.251 s, 338,924 B 1.542 s, 678,924 B 4.597 s (time roughly 3-6x per doubling). The same algorithm using pattern.match(raw, index) takes 0.082, 0.243 and 0.539 s with identical output. It is latent: 0 RTF files are held while SAFLII is blocked (D-001), but inbox and legacy imports can supply RTF judgments of 1 MB or more.
findings.how: Add module-level `_RTF_CTRL_RE = re.compile(r"\\([a-zA-Z]+)(-?\d+)?[ ]?")` and call `_RTF_CTRL_RE.match(raw, index)`. Because match.end() is then absolute, change `index += match.end()` (line 112) to `index = match.end()`.
findings.expected_impact: Linear time: 8.5x faster at 679 KB, growing with size (a 1.4 MB RTF goes from roughly 18 s to about 1 s).
findings.proving_test: Assert identical output between the old and new rtf_to_text on the existing RTF fixtures and on generated RTF with \par, \'e9, 舗 and fonttbl groups, plus a scaling test asserting a 1 MB RTF parses in under 2 s.

findings.title: Navigator corpus fixtures rebuild SQLite and FTS for every test
findings.what: `corpus` (test_navigator.py:212) and `server` (test_navigator_phase2.py:224) are function-scoped. Each use runs build_corpus, which creates the corpus schema (WAL executescript), writes text files and rebuilds an FTS index. That is 13 builds per run (5 corpus uses plus 8 server uses, counting parametrisations), and no test mutates the corpus.
findings.why: build_corpus measured 0.29-0.37 s standalone (executescript 0.089 s, close 0.045 s). Pytest setup durations were 0.55-0.89 s per use in test_navigator.py and 0.66-3.29 s in phase2.
findings.how: Make both fixtures module-scoped using tmp_path_factory.mktemp('corpus'). NavigatorServer is stateless apart from a fixed `today`, and tests that write files (facts, --save) already use their own tmp_path. If needed, keep a function-scoped variant for any future test that mutates the corpus.
findings.expected_impact: 13 builds become 2, saving about 4-8 s per run under current load.
findings.proving_test: Both navigator files pass unchanged; `pytest --setup-show` shows a single setup of each fixture per module.

findings.title: Evidence query computes snippet() for 10x over-fetched rows, then N+1 eligibility lookups
findings.evidence:
"""SELECT doc_id, title, snippet(docs, 6, '[', ']', ' ... ', 20)
                   FROM docs WHERE docs MATCH ? ORDER BY bm25(docs) LIMIT ?""",
                (query, limit * 10),
findings.what: find() fetches limit*10 = 30 ranked rows with snippet() over the full body (Act copies run to about 1 MB), then runs one eligibility query per row (line 92) and keeps at most 3. It also opens two new read-only connections per issue.
findings.why: Measured on the real index: snippet+bm25 vs bm25-only per issue query, in seconds: 0.041 vs 0.008, 0.131 vs 0.026, 0.094 vs 0.021, 0.117 vs 0.024, 0.064 vs 0.016, so 4-5x of the query cost goes on snippets that are thrown away. Each assessment runs 1-2 issues.
findings.how: Select only doc_id (and title) ordered by bm25 with the same over-fetch. Check eligibility in one `WHERE doc_id IN (...)` query, keeping rank order in Python. Then compute snippet() only for the kept rows (`... WHERE docs MATCH ? AND doc_id IN (?,?,?)`). Results stay the same: same ranking, filters and snippet arguments.
findings.expected_impact: About 4-5x less FTS time per issue (about 0.1 s saved per issue under current load); a few ms on an idle machine.
findings.proving_test: test_corpus_evidence_filters_drafts_types_and_act_copies and the malformed-query test pass; add an equality test of find() hits and snippets between the old and new query on the fixture corpus.

verdicts.reasoning: I checked the import line in all three modules: cli.py:7, ccma/cli.py:14 and navigator/cli.py:8 each have `from __future__ import annotations`. I profiled typer.main.get_command(app) with cProfile. Nearly all of its 2.13 s went into 50 get_type_hints/inspect.signature(eval_str=True) calls from typer/utils.py:107 get_params_from_function, made up of 500 builtins.eval (1.036 s) and 250 builtins.compile (1.002 s) calls across 25 commands. I then swapped in resolved annotations (cb.__annotations__ = get_type_hints(cb)): get_command went from 0.445-3.149 s to 0.021-0.027 s. I also executed all three module sources in memory with the future import removed. They imported cleanly, get_command took 0.020-0.023 s, and CliRunner `navigate provisions --help` and `ccma --help` both exited 0. So every annotation evaluates at def time. pyproject.toml has no ruff required-imports setting that would put the line back. One caveat on size: the cost depends on machine load. Unloaded get_command was 0.19-0.27 s, and 1-3 s under load. On this interpreter compile() takes 0.5-3.4 ms per call even under `python -I -S`, far above a typical CPython. The win is real for this user on every CLI invocation and every CliRunner test, but the 99.8x figure applies to this machine only.
verdicts.fix_notes: Delete the line `from __future__ import annotations` in exactly three files: src/labour_corpus/cli.py:7, src/labour_corpus/ccma/cli.py:14 and src/labour_corpus/navigator/cli.py:8. Leave it in every other module. No other edit is needed: the in-memory exec confirmed that all module-level and def-time annotations (Path, str|None, tuple[int,int]|None, frozenset[str], list[str]|None, Console, CrawlSettings, CorpusStore, CaseFacts, InMemorySource, date) resolve at import. Regression test, deterministic with no timing: in tests/test_navigator.py (or a new small test), walk labour_corpus.cli.app recursively (registered_commands[*].callback, then registered_groups[*].typer_instance) and assert `not any(isinstance(a, str) for cb in callbacks for a in cb.__annotations__.values())`. That stops a later edit from silently re-adding the import. Then run python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests/test_navigator.py, tests/test_navigator_phase2.py and tests/test_ccma_engine.py; they cover all CLI sub-apps. verdicts.reasoning: The code matches the claim. navigator/mcp_server.py:99 builds `Navigator(corpus_source(self.corpus_root), finder)` and :112 builds `source = corpus_source(self.corpus_root)` on every call, so CorpusSource._cache (grounding.py:70) is always empty. Each call reopens the database (grounding.py:78-87), reads each text file (:93) and re-normalises it (:94). On the real corpus, NavigatorServer.call_tool('navigator_assess') took 0.556-0.766 s per call and navigator_provisions took 0.651-0.737 s. The same assessment with a warm, reused source took 2.8-3.0 ms, and provisions took 6.5 ms. The cache held LRA 3 copies (1,054,297 chars) and EEA 5 copies (182,198 chars). Two corrections. Priority: this is roughly 0.6 s of latency per tool call, not a defect, so it belongs in Next Sprint rather than Do Now. Invalidation: the proposed key is weaker than it looks. The database runs in WAL mode (pragma journal_mode = wal; corpus.sqlite-wal exists), so corpus.sqlite's mtime does not move on commit. MAX(updated_at) has one-second resolution (utc_now_iso, state.py) and does not reflect deleted rows. A safer design keeps the cheap SQL query on every call, so the set of held, non-draft, readable copies is always current (D-018, D-022), and caches only the normalised text per file identity.
verdicts.fix_notes: Cache normalised text by file identity, not the whole source. (1) In grounding.py, give CorpusSource an optional shared `text_cache: dict[str, tuple[int, int, str]] | None` (doc_id -> (st_mtime_ns, st_size, normalised)). In texts_for, keep running the existing read-only SELECT on every call. For each row, stat paths.text/f'{doc_id}.txt'. If the cache has the same (mtime_ns, size), reuse its text; otherwise read, normalise and store. Leave the per-instance _cache as it is so CLI behaviour does not change. (2) In NavigatorServer.__init__, create self._text_cache = {}. In _assess and _provisions, build CorpusSource(CorpusPaths(root), text_cache=self._text_cache) when corpus_db exists, else None, keeping corpus_source's None semantics. The substring check in ground() still runs on every call. Tests in tests/test_navigator_phase2.py, using a fresh function-scoped `server` from build_corpus: (a) call navigator_provisions twice while counting calls through monkeypatch.setattr('labour_corpus.navigator.grounding.normalise', counting_wrapper); assert the second call normalises only the 21 needles and no held text. (b) Rewrite the lra text file with statute_text(LRA, drop='lra_192_2') (different size); the next navigator_assess reports that provision as not_found. (c) Insert a second non-draft LRA row plus its text file; copies_checked rises to 2 with no server restart. (d) Insert a draft row; it stays excluded. Do not cache the SQL result.

verdicts.reasoning: tagger.py:97-102 runs pattern.search(text) and then, for patterns that matched, pattern.finditer(text) from offset 0, for each of 393 compiled patterns (I counted 393, all starting with `\b`). tag_document (tagger.py:213-223) runs every tag on the full text, and both pipeline.py:324 and ccma/extract.py:230 call it. On the largest held text (b22db1dc..., 1,075,818 chars), search() alone over every 20th pattern (20 patterns) took 1.96 s, which extrapolates to about 38.5 s for search alone. Add the finditer re-scan for matched patterns and 65.9 s per document is plausible. One correction to the mechanism: the patterns are compiled with re.IGNORECASE (tagger.py:85), and sre never builds a literal or charset prefix from a cased letter under IGNORECASE. Removing `\b` would therefore not turn on prefix search. The step-2 gain comes from a cheaper failure at each position. My micro test on the same text: `\bzzqx` (I) 0.091 s, `zzqx` (I) 0.049 s, `z(?<!\w\w)zqx` (I) 0.038 s, about 2.4x. Step 2 is an exact rewrite, since `\b` before a letter means 'previous char is not \w'. Step 1 helps only patterns that matched (3 of the 20 sampled). Step 3 means pulling mandatory literals out of arbitrary regexes, which carries a precision risk under D-005, so the change as a whole needs review and should not be auto-applied. findings.title: AIA trust gate accepts any certificate whose issuer name matches a root (no signature check)
findings.what: _intermediate_is_trusted first tries build_client_verifier().verify(candidate, []). That always fails for a CA certificate ('basicConstraints.cA must not be asserted in an EE certificate', tested), so the name-only fallback at line 162 decides every time. A forged CA certificate that copies a certifi root's subject as its issuer is accepted (tested: True).
findings.why: D-013's security property ('verifies that the intermediate chains to a root certifi already trusts') is not enforced. Someone positioned between the crawler and the host can attack it in four steps. Present any bad certificate: 'certificate verify failed' alone triggers chain completion. Supply a leaf with an AIA URL they control; it is read over an unverified handshake and fetched over plain HTTP. Serve a forged CA. It then gets appended to db/tls/{host}.pem, and Python 3.13's default VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN (tested on) makes it a trust anchor. The forged CA then lets them intercept that host and silently alter statute text, and the bundle is reused on every later run.
findings.how: Replace the gate. Load the roots, keep those whose subject equals candidate.issuer, and accept only if candidate.verify_directly_issued_by(root) succeeds. Also require BasicConstraints ca=True and a current validity window. Delete the client-verifier attempt, which can never succeed for a CA. Optionally, also verify the server leaf with PolicyBuilder().store(Store(roots)).build_server_verifier(DNSName(host)).verify(leaf, [intermediate]). Tested in memory: verify_directly_issued_by accepts the real cached Certum intermediate and rejects the forged one.
findings.expected_impact: Closes a persistent interception path into the per-host trust store (1 host cached today: www.ccma.org.za). The existing cached bundle checks out: its one extra certificate is correctly signed by Certum Trusted Root CA.
findings.proving_test: tests/test_tls.py: (1) build an EC-signed CA cert whose issuer = certifi root[0].subject and assert _intermediate_is_trusted(pem) is False; (2) generate a test root and a root-signed intermediate, monkeypatch certifi.where to a bundle holding that root, and assert True. Today every test monkeypatches _intermediate_is_trusted, so the gate itself is untested.

findings.title: Chain-completion bundle: trust anchors via PARTIAL_CHAIN, reused forever, triggered by any verify failure
findings.what: There are three weaknesses. (1) A cached {host}.pem is trusted on sight, with no re-validation and no expiry, and freezes a certifi snapshot. Currently it is identical to certifi 2026.07.22 plus 1 intermediate, but later root removals will not reach that host. (2) http.py:213 passes verify=str(bundle). httpx 0.28 turns that into ssl.create_default_context(cafile=...) (and warns it is deprecated), which on Python 3.13 sets VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN, so any non-root certificate in the bundle becomes a trust anchor. (3) INCOMPLETE_CHAIN_MARKERS includes the generic 'certificate verify failed' (line 44), so a self-signed or interception certificate also triggers the AIA path (tested: True).
findings.why: These are what turn the gate defect (sec-tls-forged-intermediate) into a lasting compromise. Even with the gate fixed, a single bad write to db/tls stays trusted with no further checks.
findings.how: Build the per-host context explicitly: ctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=bundle); ctx.verify_flags &= ~ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN; then httpx.Client(verify=ctx). On cache hit, re-run the fixed gate on the bundle's non-certifi certificates and rebuild when certifi.where() is newer than the bundle. Narrowing the trigger to 'unable to get local issuer certificate' changes the deliberate test at test_tls.py:27, so it needs the owner's agreement.
findings.expected_impact: Only certifi roots can anchor a chain; a poisoned or stale bundle cannot outlive one run.
findings.proving_test: Assert Fetcher._chain_clients[host] context has verify_flags without VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN; a cached bundle containing a forged certificate is rejected and rebuilt by complete_chain.

The same pin is at pyproject.toml:34. The installed pytest is 9.1.1. Separately, `pip show labour-corpus` lists 12 requirements without certifi and cryptography, although pyproject.toml:27-28 declares them: the editable install predates that change.
findings.why: A fresh Linux or CI install from requirements.txt gets the vulnerable version, and the tested environment (9.1.1) differs from the pins. If cryptography were missing, TLS chain completion would quietly do nothing (tls.py import guards).
findings.how: Pin pytest==9.1.1 (the tested version) in requirements.txt and pyproject [test], then run `pip install -e .[test]` to refresh the metadata. Add `uvx pip-audit -r requirements.txt --disable-pip --no-deps` to CI. The resolving mode currently fails on orjson==3.12.0 in pip-audit's temp venv.
findings.expected_impact: 0 known advisories on the pinned set; pins match the installed test environment; package metadata declares certifi and cryptography.
findings.proving_test: uvx pip-audit -r requirements.txt --disable-pip --no-deps reports 'No known vulnerabilities found'; python -m pip show labour-corpus lists certifi and cryptography; targeted test files still pass under pytest 9.1.1.

findings.title: CCMA URL guard allows non-default ports and https-to-http downgrade on allow-listed hosts
findings.evidence:
if parsed.scheme not in {"https", "http"}:
        raise UrlRejected(f"scheme {parsed.scheme or '(none)'!r} is not fetchable: {url}")
findings.what: validate_url accepted 'https://www.gov.za:8443/documents/a.pdf' and 'http://www.gov.za/documents/a.pdf' (tested). All 7 base_urls in ccma_sources.yaml are https, so neither case is needed. The post-redirect check (scrape.py:85) therefore lets an https source quietly end on plain HTTP.
findings.why: A downgrade means statute or gazette bytes arrive without integrity, and an interceptor could alter them before they are checksummed and held as law. Other ports reach services the operator never allow-listed.
findings.how: Require parsed.scheme == 'https' (or equal to the scheme of the source's base_url) and parsed.port in (None, 443). Raise UrlRejected otherwise. Add both to the docstring's list of refusals.
findings.expected_impact: Rejects the 2 accepted bypass forms measured; no current source is affected (7/7 are https).
findings.proving_test: tests/test_ccma_official.py: validate_url raises UrlRejected for 'http://www.gov.za/...' and 'https://www.gov.za:8443/...'; load_allowlist(ccma_sources.yaml) still succeeds.

findings.title: DOCX bodies are decompressed with no size or ratio limit (50 MB compressed cap only)
findings.what: python-docx reads every zip part fully (_ZipPkgReader.blob_for = self._zipf.read(...), inspected). The only limit is MAX_BODY_BYTES = 50 MB on the compressed body, and deflate can expand roughly 1000x. XXE is not a risk: oxml_parser uses resolve_entities=False.
findings.why: One crafted .docx from an allow-listed host or the operator inbox can exhaust memory and end a parse run, which D-008's per-document catch does not prevent (MemoryError or a hard OOM kill).
findings.how: Before Document(...), open zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(body)). Refuse if sum(i.file_size) exceeds 200 MB, any part is over 100 MB, or file_size/compress_size exceeds 200, and report it as UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT with a note.
findings.expected_impact: Bounds decompressed DOCX memory to about 200 MB, from up to about 50 GB in theory.
findings.proving_test: Build an in-memory zip with a [Content_Types].xml plus a 300 MB zero-filled word/document.xml (ZIP_DEFLATED, about 300 KB) and assert extract_text returns UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT without allocating the payload.

verdicts.reasoning: Read tls.py:132-165 and http.py:181-215, 241-268. Ran a scratch script (scratchpad/tls_check.py) against cryptography 50.0.1, certifi 2026.07.22 and Python 3.13.15. (1) The client-verifier attempt at tls.py:152-153 fails for the real cached Certum DV TLS G2 R39 CA in db/tls/www.ccma.org.za.pem with 'basicConstraints.cA must not be asserted in an EE certificate', so the name-only fallback at tls.py:162 (`return any(root.subject == candidate.issuer for root in roots)`) makes every decision. (2) A forged CA whose issuer name is copied from certifi roots[0], self-signed with a fresh EC key and carrying BasicConstraints ca=True, returns True from _intermediate_is_trusted. (3) verify_directly_issued_by accepts the real Certum intermediate against its root and rejects the forged one with InvalidSignature. (4) ssl.create_default_context(cafile=bundle) has VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN set, and httpx 0.28.1 create_ssl_context turns verify=<str> into exactly that call. So a forged CA written to the bundle becomes a trust anchor for the host. (5) looks_like_incomplete_chain returns True for a self-signed-certificate error, so any verify failure on robots.txt (http.py:259) starts the AIA path. The AIA URL comes from a leaf read with CERT_NONE (tls.py:65-67) and is fetched over plain HTTP with follow_redirects=True (tls.py:106). The bundle is reused on later runs (tls.py:175-179). The attack needs an on-path attacker during a run, but the gate is the core property D-013 promises ('verifies that the intermediate chains to a root certifi already trusts'), and it is not enforced. Existing tests (test_tls.py:48-87) monkeypatch the gate itself, so none of them exercises it.
verdicts.fix_notes: Rewrite _intermediate_is_trusted(pem) in src/labour_corpus/tls.py:132-165. (a) Load the candidate and the certifi roots; return False on any load error. (b) Require a BasicConstraints extension with ca=True: catch x509.ExtensionNotFound and return False. Optionally, if a KeyUsage extension is present, require key_cert_sign. (c) Require not_valid_before_utc <= now <= not_valid_after_utc, with now = datetime.now(timezone.utc). (d) For each root whose root.subject == candidate.issuer, try candidate.verify_directly_issued_by(root) and return True on the first success. Catch InvalidSignature, ValueError, TypeError and UnsupportedAlgorithm per root and continue, because several roots can share a subject (re-keyed or cross-signed). (e) Otherwise return False. Delete the build_client_verifier attempt: it can never succeed for a CA certificate. Keep the ImportError -> False behaviour. Do not change complete_chain, the markers or the caching here (see sec-tls-bundle-hardening). Regression tests in tests/test_tls.py, generating certificates in memory with cryptography: (1) a forged CA whose issuer is copied from a real certifi root subject, self-signed with its own EC key and ca=True, gives _intermediate_is_trusted(...) False. This test fails today. (2) Positive case: generate a test root CA, write its PEM to tmp_path, monkeypatch.setattr(tls.certifi, 'where', lambda: str(root_pem)), sign an intermediate with ca=True using the root's key, assert True. (3) The same intermediate with ca=False gives False. (4) An expired intermediate gives False. (5) Optionally, the real cached Certum intermediate (load the last certificate of data/corpus/db/tls/www.ccma.org.za.pem read-only, skip if absent) gives True. Then run python -m pytest -q -p no:cacheprovider tests/test_tls.py. Edge: certifi roots currently emit CryptographyDeprecationWarning for negative serials. If a future cryptography raises instead, loading fails and the gate returns False, which fails safe.

verdicts.reasoning: Read http.py:164-168 and :209-214 (both clients use follow_redirects=True) and http.py:307-393. fetch() runs check_policy only on the original URL, and httpx then follows every hop. Read ccma/scrape.py:82-85: the guard runs after fetch returns. Read sources/crawler.py:196-251: final_url is never checked. Reproduced with MockTransport: www.gov.za/documents/a.pdf -> 302 http://169.254.169.254/... -> 302 https://other.example/judgments/x.pdf. The requests sent were robots(www.gov.za), the document, the IP literal over plain HTTP, and other.example. No request was made to other.example/robots.txt even though the mock robots there is 'Disallow: /'. validate_url rejected only afterwards. The claim is therefore correct: redirect targets bypass robots, Content-Signal, paid-host and trip checks, and the main crawler would store such a body under the original URL. I corrected the severity and priority. Measured over all 397 data/corpus/raw/**/fetch_meta.json: 0 cross-host and 0 scheme-changing redirects, so the defect is latent, not realised. The SSRF angle (169.254.169.254) matters little for a local-first desktop tool. The fix is a manual redirect loop touching retry, conditional GET and gap recording, which is M effort and not the cheap 'Do Now' kind. One small inaccuracy: httpx reads intermediate redirect bodies in full with no cap, so they are not 'up to 50 MB'.
verdicts.fix_notes: Not for auto-fix: it changes the fetch semantics shared by the crawler and the CCMA engine. Design notes for the owner: build both clients with follow_redirects=False. In Fetcher.fetch, loop up to 5 hops. On a 3xx with Location, resolve it with urljoin, call self.check_policy(next_url), which covers robots, Content-Signal, paid-host and trip state for the new host, plus an optional url_guard callback (LiveGetter passes partial(validate_url, hosts=..., allowed_paths=...)), and only then request it. Send If-None-Match and If-Modified-Since on the first hop only. Return final_url as today. Map refusals on a hop to the same exceptions so crawler._fetch records a gap. Tests: extend test_ccma_engine.py:188-202 so the MockTransport handler records requests and the test asserts 'elsewhere.example' was never requested. Add a crawler-level test where an off-host redirect target whose robots says Disallow is not fetched and is recorded as robots_disallow.

verdicts.reasoning: All three sub-claims check out. (1) tls.py:175-179 returns any non-empty cached {host}.pem with no re-validation or expiry. The live bundle starts byte-for-byte with the current certifi file and has 122 certificates (121 certifi roots + 1 intermediate), so it is a frozen certifi snapshot. (2) http.py:213 passes verify=str(bundle). httpx 0.28.1 create_ssl_context maps that to ssl.create_default_context(cafile=...) and emits a DeprecationWarning (source printed). On Python 3.13.15 that context has VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN set (tested), so a non-root certificate in the bundle acts as a trust anchor. (3) INCOMPLETE_CHAIN_MARKERS at tls.py:44 includes the generic 'certificate verify failed'. A self-signed error matches (tested). Real hostname-mismatch and expired errors also contain 'certificate verify failed: ...', so the 'hostname mismatch' negative test at test_tls.py:37 does not reflect the real error text. test_tls.py:27 asserts the generic marker on purpose. The present bundle is not compromised: its one extra certificate verifies by signature against Certum Trusted Root CA. The value is that, after the gate fix, bundles written under the old name-only gate would otherwise stay trusted forever. Removing PARTIAL_CHAIN keeps the real chain working, because leaf -> Certum DV TLS G2 R39 CA -> self-signed Certum Trusted Root CA are all in the store.
verdicts.fix_notes: Needs the owner. Narrowing the trigger contradicts the deliberate test at test_tls.py:27, and cache invalidation is a design choice. Suggested shape after sec-tls-forged-intermediate lands: (a) in http.py:209-214 build ctx = ssl.create_default_context(cafile=str(bundle)); ctx.verify_flags &= ~ssl.VERIFY_X509_PARTIAL_CHAIN; then httpx.Client(verify=ctx, ...). This also removes the httpx DeprecationWarning. (b) On a cache hit in complete_chain, re-run the fixed gate on every bundle certificate whose SHA-256 is not in certifi. Rebuild the bundle when that fails or when certifi.where() is newer than the bundle. (c) Optionally drop 'certificate verify failed' from the markers or require 'unable to get local issuer certificate' / 'unable to verify the first certificate', and update test_tls.py:27 by agreement.

verdicts.reasoning: Read http.py:251-252: robots.txt is fetched with client.get(), and response.content buffers the whole body with no cap. Read tls.py:101-114: httpx.get(url, follow_redirects=True), then the 64 KiB check runs only after response.content is fully in memory. Document fetches stream with a cap (http.py:365-373), so the inconsistency is real. Impact is low. Robots requests go only to a dozen allow-listed government hosts. In the AIA case the attacker is already on-path, and sec-tls-forged-intermediate is the far bigger issue there. A memory DoS needs a hostile or badly misconfigured server, so priority is lowered to Backlog. Of the proposed fix, the follow_redirects=False change for AIA could break legitimate CA AIA URLs that redirect, so it needs a decision and should be left out of an auto-fix. The size caps alone are safe: RFC 9309 lets a parser stop after at least 500 KiB.
verdicts.fix_notes: Add ROBOTS_MAX_BYTES = 512 * 1024. In robots_for (both the first attempt at http.py:251 and the retry at :261), use `with self._client_for(host).stream('GET', robots_url, timeout=self.timeout) as response:` and accumulate iter_bytes() until the limit. If truncated, cut the buffer at the last b'\n' so a partial final line is not parsed, then call parse_robots(host, response.status_code, buf). Keep the httpx.HTTPError handling unchanged; stream raises the same errors on connect. In tls._download, use `with httpx.stream('GET', url, timeout=CHAIN_TIMEOUT, follow_redirects=True) as r:`, return None for a non-200 status, and return None as soon as the accumulated size exceeds MAX_INTERMEDIATE_BYTES. Do not change redirect behaviour here. Tests: (1) in tests/test_robots.py or test_tls.py, a MockTransport serving robots.txt as a generator stream of 10 MB that counts the bytes yielded: assert robots_for returns rules, a 'Disallow: /x' in the first 1 KiB is honoured, and fewer than ~1 MB was consumed. (2) monkeypatch httpx.stream (or use a transport) so _download gets a 1 MB body: assert None is returned. The existing tests/test_tls.py and tests/test_robots.py must pass.

verdicts.reasoning: Read pipeline.py:194-224. `document = Document(io.BytesIO(body))` at line 203 runs with no size check. Inspected the installed python-docx 1.2.0. opc/phys_pkg.py:83 `return self._zipf.read(pack_uri.membername)` decompresses each part fully into memory. opc/pkgreader.py _walk_phys_parts reads every part reachable through the relationship graph (attacker-controlled), not literally every zip member, which does not change the conclusion. Measured the 14 OOXML packages in data/: max total uncompressed 1.1 MB and max part 0.6 MB, so caps in the hundreds of MB carry no recall risk. Sources are allow-listed government hosts and the operator inbox, so likelihood is low and Backlog is right.
verdicts.fix_notes: Before Document(...), inside the existing try, open `zf = zipfile.ZipFile(io.BytesIO(body))`. BadZipFile is already caught. Compute infos = zf.infolist(). Apply the ratio test only to large parts, so small repetitive XML parts are never refused. On refusal, append a note such as 'docx refused: declared uncompressed size exceeds safety limits' and return '', None, TextStatus.UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT, notes. Keep the constants at module level. Feed it through the same extraction function used by existing docx tests and assert UNSUPPORTED_FORMAT plus the note, without calling python-docx; a monkeypatched docx.Document that raises if called proves this. review.summary: The wheel itself is lean: 78 entries, 210 KB, only .py files and metadata, and no tests/ or data/ leak into either the wheel or the sdist. Most of the waste is in two other places. First, the generated FTS index is 39.45 MB. Running FTS5 'optimize' plus VACUUM brings it to 27.29 MB (-31%) with identical query results; detail=column is not an option because it breaks every navigator phrase query. Second, the documented install path (requirements.txt) pulls about 501 MB, against a 67.9 MB core closure. beautifulsoup4 is never imported (-1.09 MB). lxml is never imported directly but is still needed by python-docx. cryptography (12.64 MB with cffi and pycparser) is only imported lazily, with a fail-closed fallback, in tls.py. Separately, the package only works as an editable install: four default data paths resolve outside the wheel, and load_registry raises ConfigError from a wheel install. The installed environment has also drifted from the pins: pytest 9.1.1 vs 8.4.2, lint tools missing, and stale site-packages metadata.

findings.title: FTS rebuild never merges segments or reclaims pages: the index is 31% larger than it needs to be
findings.what: FtsIndex.rebuild() empties a regular-content FTS5 table in place, reinserts every document, and commits (line 103). It never runs INSERT INTO docs(docs) VALUES('optimize') or VACUUM. The live index has 10 segments and 275 free pages. Simulating further 'index' runs on a copy holds the file at 39.45 MB, with 8 segments and 1,366 free pages (5.6 MB).
findings.why: 39.45 MB is spent indexing 20.18 MB of text. Optimize plus VACUUM on a copy gives 27.29 MB with one segment, and returns identical doc_ids and snippets for the navigator evidence phrase queries and a plain term query. A smaller file means less disk use and a warmer page cache for the read-only navigator and search. Other schema options are worse: detail=column saves another 5.3 MB but makes every phrase query fail ('fts5: phrase queries are not supported (detail!=full)'), including evidence.py's queries and search()'s quoted-phrase fallback; prefix='2 3' grows the index to 34.99 MB.
findings.how: After the insert loop in rebuild(), run self.conn.execute("INSERT INTO docs(docs) VALUES('optimize')") and commit, then self.conn.execute('VACUUM'), which must run outside a transaction. review.summary: The layering is sound: shared fetcher and policy, rules-as-code navigator, read-only consumers. But the boundaries between the stores are informal. The navigator re-derives "which documents are the Act" from titles, so the DEL/MIBCO/EEA material it groups as "held copies" includes fund rules, a summary, a form and a code, and the "older consolidations" note is printed on all 21 provisions when it is true for 5. Neither SQLite store has a schema version (user_version = 0 on both), and a read-only consumer crashes on an older schema; the main `parse` command breaks D-008, so one bad PDF aborts it, and `rebuild_corpus.sh` hides that failure. findings.title: `parse` violates D-008: one bad PDF aborts the whole re-parse, and rebuild_corpus.sh hides it
findings.what: The per-document loop of `parse` catches only three exception types. Its siblings catch Exception at the document boundary: crawler._collect (crawler.py:292) and ccma harvest._seed (harvest.py:461). pypdf's PdfReadError and LimitReachedError do not subclass ValueError, and pdf.py's page loop (line 71) does not catch IndexError, AttributeError or LimitReachedError. Reproduced in a scratch corpus: a PDF whose page extraction raises IndexError makes `parse` exit 1 with 0 rows written, and the healthy HTML document after it is never parsed. Paths are processed in sorted order with no checkpoint, so every re-run dies at the same file. rebuild_corpus.sh sets only `set -u` and pipes every stage through tail or grep, so a failing stage returns status 0 and the script still prints '=== REBUILD COMPLETE ===' (demonstrated), then indexes and reports a half-reparsed corpus.
findings.why: Whole-corpus re-parses are how parser fixes land (D-014, D-024). A single malformed government PDF would block them permanently, and the operator would see a success banner.
findings.how: Catch Exception (noqa BLE001, with a D-008 comment) around the per-document body at cli.py:396-463, logging to ERRORS.jsonl and recording a parse_failed gap as crawler._collect does. Change rebuild_corpus.sh to `set -euo pipefail`. Optionally add IndexError, AttributeError and LimitReachedError to pdf.py's per-page catch so one bad page costs one page. Follow-up (M): move the per-document re-parse, including the duplicated OCR-apply blocks at lines 416-434 and 437-457, into pipeline.reparse_stored(). That cuts cli.parse from complexity 18 / 101 statements and lets `ccma seed` reuse the OCR sidecar.
findings.expected_impact: One bad file costs one document instead of the run. The repro goes from exit 1 with 0 rows to 1 failure logged and the other documents parsed. Rebuild failures become visible.
findings.proving_test: CliRunner test: two raw/ docs (PDF, HTML); monkeypatch pypdf.PageObject.extract_text to raise IndexError; assert exit 0, the HTML row is present, and ERRORS.jsonl names the PDF. Shell check: a stage exiting 1 makes rebuild_corpus.sh exit non-zero.

findings.title: link_held_citations is O(known x documents): no index on documents.neutral_citation
findings.evidence:

WHERE d.neutral_citation = known_citations.neutral_citation
findings.what: link_held_citations runs two correlated subqueries (SET and EXISTS) per known citation against documents.neutral_citation. The SCHEMA indexes documents only on url+sha, forum+year, source and doc_type. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows SCAN known_citations, then a correlated SCAN d twice. One EXISTS pass over 6,410 refs x 397 docs takes 1.96 s read-only, and the full call takes 1.47 s on a scratch copy. It is called by import-citation-map and import-legacy-documents and is needed after every case-law ingest.

findings.expected_impact: Measured 1.47 s -> 0.06 s (24x) now. The plan becomes SEARCH d USING COVERING INDEX, which is O(K log D) at any scale.

findings.what: Both stores report PRAGMA user_version = 0. CorpusStore._migrate adds three documents columns, and only when a writer opens the DB. findings.title: CCMA catalogue seed is quadratic: each FTS delete fully scans an UNINDEXED key
findings.evidence:
c.execute(
    "DELETE FROM records_fts WHERE source=? AND native_id=?",
    (row.source, row.native_id),
findings.what: records_fts declares source and native_id UNINDEXED (lines 76-79), and knowledge_fts declares id UNINDEXED. Every non-skipped upsert_record, including a first insert, deletes by those columns. replace_knowledge_for and replace_scenarios delete per unit id (lines 347 and 360). The plan is 'SCAN records_fts VIRTUAL TABLE INDEX 0:', a full scan. Measured per-upsert cost: 224 / 380 / 575 / 717 ms at 500 / 1,000 / 2,000 / 4,000 records. At 4,000 rows the delete alone takes 433 ms by key against 4.4 ms by rowid. find_local_corpus (find.py:38-44) imports every held judgment, without the 'reviews a CCMA award' selection report.py:147-149 claims, so opening case law pushes about 6,410 records through this path.
findings.why: Seeding n records costs O(n^2). About 0.11 ms per existing row means roughly 37 minutes of delete scans alone for 6,410 judgments, against about 30 s keyed by rowid, and every later re-seed pays O(n) per record.
findings.how: Key the FTS rows by an explicit integer. Either add `fts_rowid INTEGER UNIQUE` to records and knowledge_units, or use a side table (source, native_id) -> rowid. Insert with `INSERT INTO records_fts(rowid, ...)` and delete with `WHERE rowid = ?`. Batch commits per source instead of per record (Catalogue.tx commits on every call). Ship it as a catalogue migration that rebuilds both FTS tables (depends on arch-schema-version). Either enforce the related_authority selection the report claims or reword the report.
findings.expected_impact: Per-record delete about 100x cheaper at 4k rows, flat as the catalogue grows. Case-law-scale seed is minutes, not about an hour.
findings.proving_test: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN of the FTS delete shows a rowid constraint ('INDEX 0:='). A benchmark test shows per-upsert time at 4k records within 1.5x of 500. The idempotency tests in test_ccma_engine.py still pass.

findings.title: CCMA re-seed 'skips' on 4 fields, so extractor and knowledge-rule fixes never reach seeded records

existing is not None
and existing["sha256"] == row.sha256
and existing["parse_status"] == row.parse_status
findings.what: upsert_record returns 'skipped' when sha256, parse_status, case_number and dispute_type match, and seed_one (seed.py:77-78) then returns before rebuilding knowledge units. findings.title: Route dispatch falls through to the EEA branch; Phase 3 tracks would be misrouted silently
findings.what: Track is a class of bare string constants (routing.py:19-23), and the engine dispatches on it through if/elif chains: _deadlines at line 105, _route at lines 117, 123 and 128-160. _route's final `else:` is EEA-specific and grounds eea_10_6_a. _deadlines adds the Labour Court referral deadline only for LABOUR_COURT and ELECTION. Phase 3 (docs/navigator-architecture.md:187-188) adds s189A, s198, s197 and s186(1)(b) routes. A new Track value missed in any chain would be routed as an EEA discrimination referral citing EEA s10(6)(a), with no Labour Court deadline. Grounding would still say 'verified', because the quote exists.
findings.why: A wrong forum or a missing deadline is the costliest error for the employee (D-022). Neither mypy nor the tests can detect non-exhaustive dispatch on plain strings.
findings.how: Make Track a StrEnum with unchanged values (golden YAML, JSON logs and tests compare strings, so they keep working). Change the last branch to `elif track is Track.EEA_LABOUR_COURT:` and add `else: assert_never(track)` in _route and _deadlines. Add a test parametrised over list(Track). findings.title: Both YAML loaders ignore unknown keys; sources.yaml defaults `enabled` to True

Neither checks the `version` field both files carry, and sources.yaml's defaults.jurisdiction is ignored. `enabled` defaults to True in sources.yaml but to False in ccma_sources.yaml (allowlist.py:305). min_delay and max_delay fall back to 1-2 s. findings.title: A persistent 5xx/429/408 on one URL aborts the entire crawl and records no gap
findings.what: Fetcher.fetch retries RETRY_STATUSES and then re-raises RetryableStatus. That class is defined at http.py:43 as `class RetryableStatus(RuntimeError)`, so it matches none of Crawler._fetch's handlers (ChallengeDetected, RobotsDisallowed, ContentSignalOptOut, HostTripped, httpx.HTTPError, OSError). It propagates through crawl_source into cli.crawl, whose try only handles KeyboardInterrupt.
findings.why: One flaky government URL (a 503 is routine on gov.za) ends a multi-hour, multi-source crawl with a traceback. Every later source is skipped, and the failing URL never becomes a gap row. This contradicts D-008 ('One malformed government PDF must never end a multi-hour crawl') and the architecture rule that refusal becomes data. No test constructs a Crawler, so nothing catches it.
findings.how: Add `except RetryableStatus as exc:` to Crawler._fetch, next to the httpx handler. It should do `outcome.failed += 1`, `self._gap(outcome, source, 'http_error', url, f'HTTP {exc.status} after retries')`, `self.log.error('fetch', str(exc), source_id=source.id, url=url)` and return None. Alternatively add RetryableStatus to the existing tuple. While there, split SourceOutcome.failed into a running total and a consecutive-failure counter. Line 242 resets it to 0 on success, so the per-source 'failed=' printed at cli.py:271 shows only the trailing streak.
findings.expected_impact: A transient-status URL costs one recorded gap instead of the whole run. Verified with MockTransport: a 503 raises RetryableStatus after 3 attempts, and none of _fetch's handlers catch it.
findings.proving_test: tests/test_idempotency.py (or a new test_crawler.py): a Crawler with Fetcher(client=httpx.Client(transport=MockTransport(...)), retry_waits=(0,), RateLimiter(0,0)) where a link_index page links two PDFs. The first PDF always returns 503 and the second returns 200. Assert crawl_source returns normally, stores 1 document, and records 1 gap of kind http_error for the 503 URL.

findings.title: robots.txt: only the first matching group is honoured, so a second '*' group's Disallow and ai-input=no are ignored
findings.what: _matching_group returns a single _Group: the first '*' group, or the first group with the longest specific token. RFC 9309 s2.2.1 says rules from all groups matching the user-agent MUST be combined. can_fetch, crawl_delay and content_signal all read only the chosen group.
findings.why: CDN-managed robots.txt files commonly prepend a `User-Agent: *` Content-Signal block above the site's own `User-agent: *` rules. In that layout the crawler ignores the site's Disallow lines and its ai-input=no reservation. That is a D-002 and robots compliance hole in http.Fetcher.check_policy, which both the corpus crawler and the CCMA engine use (D-019). Measured in memory: with two '*' groups, can_fetch('/judgments/x') is True and permits_rag_corpus() is True, despite `Disallow: /judgments/` and `ai-input=no` in the second group.
findings.how: Have _matching_group collect every group whose agent equals the best specific token length (or, if none, every '*' group) and merge them into one synthetic _Group. Concatenate allows and disallows. Take the max of any crawl_delay. Merge Content-Signal most-restrictively: any False wins for ai_input, ai_train and search. Also keep group-less `Content-Signal` lines if a host uses them.
findings.expected_impact: Closes a policy hole for every host with duplicated groups. Hosts with a single group behave exactly as now. It only ever makes the crawler more restrictive.
findings.proving_test: tests/test_robots.py: parse_robots('example.org', 200, two '*' groups as above). Assert can_fetch(UA, '/judgments/x') is False, content_signal(UA).permits_rag_corpus() is False, and '/other' is still allowed. Add a second case with two groups for the bot token, whose disallows must merge.

Measured on Python 3.13: 'inf', '1e12' and even '1e11' all make RateLimiter.wait raise OverflowError ('timestamp out of range for C PyTime_t'). That is not RetryableStatus or TransportError, so tenacity re-raises it (403), and Crawler._fetch (crawler.py:224) does not catch OverflowError (an ArithmeticError, not an OSError). The crawl crashes. Correction: '1e12' does not sleep 31,700 years; it crashes like 'inf'. A hang needs a value just below the overflow point (e.g. '1e9', about 31 years) or a long but legal integer. The HTTP-date form being ignored is real, and the crawler then retries sooner than the server asked. Malformed or hostile values are unlikely in practice and the politeness gap is modest, so Next Sprint rather than Do Now.
verdicts.fix_notes: Rewrite parse_retry_after. Strip the value. If it matches `^\d+$`, return float(int(v)). findings.title: cli.parse swaps OCR text into a document whose tags, draft flag, language and status came from an empty text layer

findings.what: `parse` (101 statements, PLR0915) calls build_parsed_doc on the scanned PDF first. Every field derived from text (dismissal/sector tags, tag_evidence, outcome, remedy, doc_type, is_draft/draft_reason, language, quotes, parse_status, citation metadata) is therefore computed from an empty string. review.summary: Storage is not where the cost is. raw/ holds 397 bodies (337.4 MB), and only 0.88 MB of that (0.26%) is byte-duplicated. There are no orphaned versions, the 27 OCR sidecars already save about 120 CPU-minutes per re-parse, and the logs grow by about 0.1 MB per crawl. The real costs are network and CPU. The 2026-09-20 crawl re-requested 33 URLs it had already handled and threw away 89.6 MB (25.8%) of what it downloaded. The main crawler ignores the 8-15 s CCMA delays that D-012 promises. findings.title: The main crawler ignores per-source delays, so CCMA would be crawled at 1-2 s instead of the documented 8-15 s
findings.what: sources.yaml values for SourceDef.min_delay/max_delay are loaded (registry.py:155-156) but never read. Neither Crawler nor the crawl command uses them: the Fetcher gets one global limiter set to the CLI defaults of 1.0/2.0 s. The three CCMA sources are access: open and enabled: true, with min_delay 8.0 and max_delay 15.0.
findings.why: D-012 and the sources.yaml comment say the CCMA delays were raised to 8-15 s so that a future run is gentler than the one that lost access. The code does not enforce this. Once access returns, the next all-sources crawl (including rebuild_corpus.sh step 1) would hit www.ccma.org.za about 8x faster than documented. That is the rate most likely to re-trigger the WAF, and it costs the public host. The CCMA publishes no robots crawl-delay that would slow it down.
findings.how: Give RateLimiter a per-host floor, e.g. a dict set by set_host_delay(host, min, max) and consulted in wait(). Call it from Crawler.crawl_source with max(settings.min_delay, source.min_delay) and the same for max_delay. Keep the robots crawl-delay as an additional floor.
findings.expected_impact: CCMA requests spaced 8-15 s apart instead of 1-2 s (~8x fewer requests per minute) once access returns. No change for the other collectable sources, which use the 1-2 s default.
findings.proving_test: New crawler test with httpx.MockTransport and SourceDef(min_delay=8, max_delay=15) linking 3 PDFs. Monkeypatch labour_corpus.http.time.sleep (and time.monotonic) to record waits, then assert every inter-request wait for that host is >= 8.0 s while a default source's waits stay within 1-2 s.
