findings.what: Crawler does not track URLs already handled in the current run. A document linked from several listing or sub-pages, or a listing reached from several sources, is requested again each time. In the 2026-09-20 RUN.jsonl there were 445 requests for 412 distinct URLs, so 33 were repeats. Of those, 21 returned 200 with a full body: all 17 MIBCO PDFs, re-reached via the /collective-agreements/?s= sub-page, plus labour.gov.za Home.aspx 4 times. That is 89.57 MB of the run's 347.4 MB. BCCEI's two agreement PDFs were conditionally re-requested 5 times each.
findings.why: Every repeat costs the public host a request (89.6 MB of bandwidth in total) and costs the operator a 1-2 s rate-limit slot plus transfer time (19.8 s measured). The result is then discarded as skipped_duplicate.
findings.how: Add to Crawler a set of document URLs handled this run and an in-memory dict of listing URL to FetchResult. In _collect, return early (bumping skipped_duplicate) when the URL is already in the set. For listings, reuse the cached body so a second source can still apply its own link_patterns without a new request. The single Crawler instance in cli.crawl spans all sources, so repeats across sources are covered too.
findings.expected_impact: 33 fewer requests (-7.4%) and 89.6 MB less transfer (-25.8%) on a from-scratch crawl of the current sources; roughly 50-70 s less wall time.
findings.proving_test: MockTransport serving robots.txt, an index linking doc.pdf, and a sub-page that also links doc.pdf: after crawl_source, assert exactly one GET for doc.pdf and outcome.stored == 1. Second case: two SourceDefs sharing one listing URL produce one listing GET, and both sources' patterns are still applied.

findings.title: The navigator MCP server reloads and re-normalises all statute copies on every tool call
findings.what: navigator_assess (line 99) and navigator_provisions (line 112) each build a new CorpusSource, which throws away its per-Act cache. Every call therefore re-queries SQLite and reads and normalises every held LRA and EEA copy (3 + 5 copies, 1.24 M characters).
findings.why: The stdio server is long-lived and this work is the same on every call. Measured on the real corpus: 2.1-4.0 s per call with a fresh source against 0.03-0.05 s with a reused one, about 60-100x. This is the main per-request compute cost and would scale directly with any future HTTP API.
findings.how: Build the CorpusSource once (lazily) in NavigatorServer and reuse it. Invalidate it when corpus.sqlite's mtime (or MAX(updated_at)) changes, so a re-parse is picked up rather than served stale.
findings.expected_impact: About 2-4 s down to about 0.04 s per tool call after the first; CPU for 100 assessments falls from roughly 3-6 min to about 5 s.
findings.proving_test: In tests/test_navigator_phase2.py, build a NavigatorServer on the tmp corpus fixture and count CorpusSource.texts_for SQLite loads (monkeypatch grounding.normalise with a counter). Two navigator_provisions calls should load once; after os.utime on corpus.sqlite, the next call should reload.

findings.title: Conditional GET never returns 304 on Apache hosts that add '-gzip' to the ETag (89.4 MB of MIBCO PDFs)
findings.what: Apache mod_deflate appends -gzip to the ETag of a compressed response and then does not match that ETag in If-None-Match. Because If-None-Match takes precedence over If-Modified-Since (RFC 9110 13.2.2), the stored Last-Modified is ignored and the full body comes back. All 17 MIBCO PDFs (Server: Apache, Content-Encoding: gzip on application/pdf) returned 200 with full bodies when re-requested with their stored validators (RUN.jsonl events 704-737). fetch_log holds -gzip ETags for 17 MIBCO documents (89.4 MB) and 53 gov.za listing pages (3.6 MB).
findings.why: Resume by validator is the project's main way of limiting load and transfer. For these hosts it silently never yields a 304, so every walk of the MIBCO listing re-downloads 89.4 MB that is then discarded as an unchanged sha256.
findings.how: When the stored ETag ends in -gzip" or -br" and a Last-Modified is stored, send If-Modified-Since only. Alternatively, send both the stored and the suffix-stripped ETag as an If-None-Match list. Keep the sha256 comparison as the backstop. On the next permitted crawl, log the status of one conditional request to one MIBCO PDF to confirm.
findings.expected_impact: Up to 89.4 MB and 17 full downloads saved per MIBCO walk, plus about 3.6 MB on gov.za listings, once confirmed live. This becomes a per-run saving if the listing-304 fix below makes listings always walk.
findings.proving_test: MockTransport test: a fetch with etag '"abc-gzip"' and a stored Last-Modified sends If-Modified-Since and no If-None-Match; a plain ETag still sends If-None-Match.

findings.title: A 304 on a listing page ends the walk, so resume and re-runs silently skip unvisited documents
findings.what: Listing pages get conditional GETs (102 of 113 listing rows carry validators) but their bodies are never stored. On a 304, _fetch returns None (line 230) and the whole subtree is skipped. MIBCO's listing honours If-None-Match (304 at RUN.jsonl event 701). If a crawl is killed after 5 of MIBCO's 17 PDFs, the resumed run gets a 304 on the listing and never collects the other 12 until the page changes. The same applies to documents that failed earlier (http_error) and to sub-pages that changed under an unchanged parent.
findings.why: This is a saving that is actually a defect. state.py promises that a killed crawl can simply be restarted, but here work is dropped with no gap recorded. It also hides how much the -gzip ETag problem costs.
findings.how: Persist listing bodies (113 pages, 11.0 MB), e.g. in db/listings/{sha256(url)}.html or a listings table, and walk the cached body on a 304. Child documents still get conditional GETs, which cost 0 bytes when unchanged. A cheaper variant is to send no validators for listing pages, at up to 11.0 MB extra per full crawl.
findings.expected_impact: Restores resume correctness at about 0 extra bytes (cache variant) or at most 11.0 MB per run (no-validator variant); documents keep their 304s.
findings.proving_test: MockTransport with Fetcher(retry_waits=(0,)). Run 1 serves the listing with ETag "L" and doc A, and returns HTTP 500 for doc B. Run 2 answers the listing with a 304. Assert that doc B is requested and stored in run 2.

findings.title: pypdf text extraction dominates parse CPU and is about 10x slower than an available alternative
findings.what: On 12 random raw PDFs, pypdf took 20.3 s against pymupdf's 1.9 s (10.6x), with nearly identical text (163,414 vs 164,434 characters). On the slowest document (MIBCO Main Agreement, 2.24 MB, 197 pages), pypdf took 69.7 s against pymupdf's 5.8 s. In the 2026-09-20 crawl, inline parse and store took about 894 s of 1,709 s wall time. An in-memory full re-parse ran 1,658 s for 332 of 397 documents under concurrent load.
findings.why: Every parse pays this cost: the in-line crawl parse, rebuild_corpus.sh step 4 and D-024-style re-parses. It is the largest recurring local compute cost; OCR is already paid once and kept in sidecars.
findings.how: Make the extractor pluggable behind extract_pdf_text. Benchmark pypdfium2 (permissive licence) alongside pymupdf, which is AGPL-3.0 and already the optional ocr extra, and choose with the licence in mind. Before switching: re-parse into a copy, diff text_chars per document, re-run the 21-provision grounding and the 30 golden cases, and record a decision.
findings.expected_impact: About 10x faster PDF extraction; estimated full-parse wall time from roughly 15-25 min down to 3-5 min for the current corpus. Tagger cost is unchanged.
findings.proving_test: Parametrised test over the generated paged_pdf fixtures: both backends give the same TextStatus and at least 99% of the characters. The real-corpus test in test_navigator still grounds 21/21 after a re-parse.

findings.title: rebuild_corpus.sh re-parses all 397 documents after crawl and legacy import have already parsed them
findings.what: Crawl (crawler._collect) and import-legacy-documents already run build_parsed_doc and persist on every new document. Step 4 then re-parses all of them again: parse walks every raw/**/fetch_meta.json (cli.py:325) with no skip. After a fresh crawl, its only additional effect is re-attaching the 27 OCR sidecars (328 pages).
findings.why: A from-scratch rebuild pays the parse cost twice: about 894 s measured in-line, then a full re-parse of more than 1,600 s under load.
findings.how: Add `parse --only-status ocr_needed` and use it in step 4. Alternatively, add `--changed-only`, which skips documents whose content_sha256 and a new PARSER_VERSION stamp are unchanged. Keep plain `parse` for deliberate re-parses after parser changes (D-024).
findings.expected_impact: About 15-25 min of CPU saved per rebuild; step 4 drops to seconds (27 sidecar reuses, no OCR outstanding today).
findings.proving_test: CLI test on a tmp corpus with one ok document and one ocr_needed document that has an ocr.txt sidecar: `parse --only-status ocr_needed` changes only the second document's updated_at and leaves it text_status ok.

findings.title: The CCMA engine re-downloads and re-parses unchanged records on every live harvest
findings.what: LiveGetter.get never passes etag or last_modified. meta.json does not keep validators. store_artifact only sees 'unchanged' after the full body has been downloaded (download.py:82-84). _download_and_seed then calls seed_one, which parses the bytes again before upsert_record returns 'skipped'.
findings.why: Each live harvest repeats the full download and parse of every held record. Today that is 1 record per run (GG 53294, 1.96 MB, 16 pages), and it grows linearly with Layer 1 sources. This departs from the resume-by-validator behaviour of the fetcher the engine is meant to reuse (D-019).
findings.how: Carry response headers in Page and store ETag/Last-Modified in meta.json. Let LiveGetter.get accept validators, and map a 304 to an 'unchanged' outcome that skips store and seed unless only the seed stage was requested.
findings.expected_impact: 0 body bytes and no re-parse for unchanged records. Today that saves 1.96 MB and one 16-page parse per run, growing to N times that as Layer 1 grows.
findings.proving_test: In test_ccma_official.py, a MockTransport returns 304 when If-None-Match matches. Over two live harvests, the second has skipped == 1, the transport saw If-None-Match, and there is no new seed_ok event.

findings.title: CCMA engine OCR: reuse the existing stored_text hook with a D-014 sidecar so the OCR runs once
findings.evidence:
if stored_text is not None:
        text, title, status = stored_text, None, TextStatus.OK if stored_text.strip() else TextStatus.EMPTY
findings.what: The missing OCR step is already in dead-code.md. The new point is that the hook already exists: parse_artifact accepts stored_text, and pipeline.load_ocr_text, pipeline.save_ocr_text and parse.ocr.ocr_pdf can be reused as they are. GG 53294, the only held Layer 1 record and the 2025 dismissal code, stays ocr_needed and is not indexed.
findings.why: OCR runs at about 22 s per page at 300 dpi, so GG 53294's 16 pages take about 6 CPU-minutes. Without a sidecar beside original.pdf, every OCR-enabled seed would repeat that work.
findings.how: In Harvester._seed and _seed_only, load an ocr.txt beside original.pdf with load_ocr_text and pass it as stored_text, with an OCR provenance note and capped confidence. Behind a new `ccma seed --ocr` flag, run ocr_pdf(body, dpi=220) once when parse_status is ocr_needed, then save_ocr_text.
findings.expected_impact: A one-off 3-6 CPU-minutes for GG 53294 (at 220-300 dpi) and 0 on every later seed; the 2025 dismissal code becomes searchable.
findings.proving_test: In test_ccma_official.py, a generated scanned PDF with a pre-written ocr.txt goes through seed_only and comes out parse_status parsed with the OCR note; ocr_pdf, monkeypatched to raise, is never called.

verdicts.reasoning: cli.py:240 builds one global `RateLimiter(settings.min_delay, settings.max_delay)`. CrawlSettings defaults are 1.0/2.0 (config.py:209-210) and the crawl command has no delay option. registry.py:155-156 loads SourceDef.min_delay/max_delay, but grep finds no reader of `source.min_delay` or `source.max_delay` anywhere in sources/ or cli.py. The only per-source use is in the CCMA engine (ccma/harvest.py:158-166, ccma/cli.py:228). Crawler.crawl_source (crawler.py:61-77) never touches the limiter. RateLimiter.wait (http.py:92-95) floors only on its own min_delay and the robots crawl_delay, and DEFAULT_CRAWL_DELAY is 1.0 (robots.py:22). sources.yaml:368-410 has all three CCMA sources as `access: open`, `enabled: true`, `min_delay: 8.0`, `max_delay: 15.0`. The comment at sources.yaml:362-364 and D-012 both rely on these delays being applied. So any all-sources crawl, including rebuild_corpus.sh step 1, paces www.ccma.org.za at 1-2 s rather than 8-15 s (mean 1.5 s against 11.5 s, about 7.7x). This does not conflict with D-012's "no slower-but-quieter crawling": D-012 itself records these delays as the intended behaviour. Today's risk is limited because CCMA answers 403 everywhere, so the host trips early. The defect bites as soon as access returns.
verdicts.fix_notes: In http.py RateLimiter (a slots dataclass), add a field `_host_delays: dict[str, tuple[float, float]] = field(default_factory=dict)` and a method `set_host_delay(self, host: str, min_delay: float, max_delay: float) -> None`. Under self._lock, it stores the element-wise max of any existing entry and the new values, so a later source on the same host can never lower the pace. In wait(), read `hmin, hmax = self._host_delays.get(host, (0.0, 0.0))` and compute `floor = max(self.min_delay, hmin, crawl_delay or 0.0)` and `ceiling = max(self.max_delay, hmax, floor)`. Leave penalise() and the first-request-returns-0 behaviour unchanged. In Crawler.crawl_source (crawler.py:61), before any fetch, call `self.fetcher.limiter.set_host_delay(source.host, source.min_delay, source.max_delay)`, and also call it for `host_of(source.base_url)` when that differs from source.host. Do not mutate the global min_delay/max_delay the way ccma/harvest.py:165 does, because that slows every other host. Tests to add to tests/test_robots.py: (1) `RateLimiter(0.01, 0.02)` with `set_host_delay('slow.example', 0.15, 0.2)`: two waits on slow.example take >= 0.14 s, and a wait on fast.example after a first call takes < 0.05 s. (2) set_host_delay called again with smaller values keeps the larger floor. (3) A crawler-level test: build a Crawler with a Fetcher over httpx.MockTransport (robots 404, empty listing) and `RateLimiter(0, 0)`, run crawl_source on a SourceDef with min_delay=8, max_delay=15, and assert `limiter._host_delays[source.host] == (8.0, 15.0)`. Also run tests/test_sources_yaml.py.

verdicts.reasoning: crawler.py:256-261: _collect always calls _fetch, and neither _crawl_one_index_page (lines 157-178) nor _collect keeps a per-run visited set. I reproduced the numbers from data/corpus/reports/RUN.jsonl. The first crawl (events 0-785, 2026-09-20T12:58-13:26) made 445 fetcher requests for 412 distinct URLs, 347.36 MB in total. Of the 33 repeats, 21 were HTTP 200 with a body: 89.57 MB and 19.8 s of transfer. The mechanism is visible in the log. MIBCO's listing /collective-agreements/ (event 666) links to itself and to ?s=, both matching the 'agreement' link pattern. The self-link got a 304 (701), but /collective-agreements/?s= (703) re-listed all 17 PDFs, which were re-fetched with full bodies (704-736), and each was then logged `parse skipped_duplicate` (705-737). labour.gov.za Home.aspx was fetched 4 extra times as a sub-page of different DEL sources (86, 149, 154, 246). BCCEI's 2 PDFs were conditionally re-requested 5 times each (757-782, all 304, but each still took a rate-limit slot). A per-run set also closes an in-run correctness hole: a listing reached by a second source in the same run is sent the validators the first source just stored, so a 304 ends the second source's walk (crawler.py:230-234 and 133-135).
verdicts.fix_notes: In Crawler.__init__, add `self._seen_docs: set[str] = set()` and `self._listings: dict[str, FetchResult | None] = {}`. At the top of _collect, if the url is in _seen_docs, bump outcome.skipped_duplicate and log.bump('skipped_duplicate'), log event('parse', source_id, url, status='skipped_duplicate_in_run') and return; otherwise add the url before fetching. Adding before the fetch gives one request per URL per run, and politeness wins over an in-run retry; tenacity already retries transient errors. For listing fetches, i.e. the three call sites at lines 82, 97, 133 and 166, route through a helper `_fetch_listing(source, url, outcome)`. It returns the cached FetchResult when the url is in _listings, so a second source applies its own link_patterns and title_filter to the cached body. Otherwise it calls _fetch and caches the result, including None. Only cache results that have a body. Do not change _fetch or the fetch_log semantics. Edge cases: the max_docs_per_source budget and the consecutive-failure counter are unaffected because skipping neither stores nor fails; the per-run set lives on the single Crawler that cli.crawl creates for all sources. Test: add tests/test_crawler.py. Build a Fetcher over httpx.MockTransport with `RateLimiter(0, 0)` that serves robots.txt 404, a listing https://h.example/list/ linking to /doc.pdf, /list/ and /list/?s=, the ?s= page linking to /doc.pdf again, and a minimal valid PDF or HTML body for /doc.pdf. Use CorpusPaths(tmp_path), CorpusStore and RunLog with CrawlSettings, and a SourceDef(kind=LINK_INDEX, link_patterns=['\\.pdf$','list']). Assert /doc.pdf is requested exactly once, outcome.stored == 1, and /list/ is requested once. Then run a second SourceDef on the same host with the same base_url and assert no new requests for /list/ or /doc.pdf.

verdicts.reasoning: The code is as claimed. mcp_server.py:99 (`Navigator(corpus_source(self.corpus_root), finder)`) and :112 (`source = corpus_source(self.corpus_root)`) each build a new CorpusSource, and its per-Act `_cache` (grounding.py:68-97) dies with it. Each texts_for call opens SQLite, reads every matching text/{doc_id}.txt and normalise()s it. I measured read-only on the real corpus: EEA 5 copies / 182,198 chars and LRA 3 copies / 1,054,297 chars, which matches the claimed 1.24 M. Grounding all 21 provisions took 1.16-1.34 s with a fresh source against 0.01 s with a reused one, about 100x. The claimed 2.1-4.0 s per call is higher than I measured; it was probably taken under concurrent load. The proposed invalidation key is also unsafe as stated: corpus.sqlite runs in WAL mode (PRAGMA journal_mode = 'wal', and -wal and -shm files are present), so the main file's mtime does not change on commit until a checkpoint, and a cache keyed on it could serve stale grounding after a re-parse. MAX(updated_at) is maintained on upsert (state.py:295) and is the correct key. This is a latency and compute waste, not a defect, so Next Sprint rather than Do Now.
verdicts.fix_notes: In NavigatorServer.__init__, add `self._source = None` and `self._source_key = None`. Add `_statutes(self)`. If corpus.sqlite does not exist, return None. Otherwise compute key = `SELECT MAX(updated_at), COUNT(*) FROM documents` over a `file:...?mode=ro` URI connection that is closed immediately; do not use file mtime, because the DB is WAL. If key != self._source_key, set `self._source = corpus_source(self.corpus_root)` and `self._source_key = key`, then return self._source. Use it at line 99 (`Navigator(self._statutes(), finder)`) and line 112. Keep corpus_source() returning None when there is no DB, so not_checked behaviour is preserved. Test in tests/test_navigator_phase2.py, using the existing `server` fixture: monkeypatch `labour_corpus.navigator.mcp_server.corpus_source` with a counting wrapper and call `server.call_tool('navigator_provisions', {})` twice; assert one construction and identical results. Then upsert a changed LRA document through CorpusStore, which bumps updated_at, call again, and assert a second construction and that the grounding reflects the new text. Also assert navigator_assess reuses the same instance.

verdicts.reasoning: http.py:320-323 sends the stored ETag as If-None-Match and Last-Modified as If-Modified-Since. A read-only fetch_log query shows 70 rows with '-gzip' ETags: www.mibco.org.za has 17 document rows, 89.40 MB, all with Last-Modified; www.gov.za has 53 listing rows, 3.65 MB, all with Last-Modified. raw/bc_mibco/undated/84724b4c.../headers.json shows `server: Apache`, `content-encoding: gzip`, `content-type: application/pdf` and `etag: "37849-63a2435e99c80-gzip"`, where 0x37849 = 227,401 is the identity size. This is the mod_deflate suffix signature. In RUN.jsonl, all 17 MIBCO PDFs were re-requested within the run after _collect had stored their validators (crawler.py:303-310), and every one came back 200 with the full body (704-736), then `skipped_duplicate`. MIBCO's HTML listing, whose ETag carries no -gzip suffix, did return 304 (701), so the host honours validators in general. The RFC 9110 precedence point is correct: If-None-Match makes the server ignore If-Modified-Since. Whether If-Modified-Since alone or a stripped ETag yields a 304 is still unmeasured, so the fix needs one live confirmation. Not auto-fixable: the IMS-only variant trades data currency (a false 304 if Last-Modified is not maintained) for bandwidth. The safer variant is `If-None-Match: "x-gzip", "x"`, which only lets the server match its own identity ETag.

crawler.py:133-135 returns when _fetch returns None, and _fetch returns None on a 304 (lines 230-234). The listing's validators are written by _fetch itself (record_fetch at 245-253) before any child document is processed. A crawl killed partway through a listing's documents therefore gets a 304 on the listing at resume and never visits the remaining documents. The same applies to the year-index path (82-84) and to sub-pages (166-168). This contradicts state.py:1-7 and README.md:207-213 ("running it again continues from where it stopped"). DB check (read-only): fetch_log has 113 rows with doc_id NULL, 102 of them with validators, 11.02 MB in total, which matches the claim. RUN.jsonl confirms MIBCO's listing honours If-None-Match (event 701: 304). Documents that failed earlier (http_error or parse_failed rows) are likewise never retried while their listing returns 304. Both fixes need a choice: persisting listing bodies is a new on-disk store, and dropping validators for listings costs bandwidth. So M and not auto-fixable.

parse/pdf.py:68-70 extracts text page by page with pypdf `page.extract_text()` (pypdf==6.19.0, pyproject.toml:24). I re-measured on 6 randomly chosen raw/**/source.pdf files (seed 7, 240 PDFs held): pypdf took 9.93 s against PyMuPDF 1.28.2's 0.87 s (11.4x), with near-identical output (123,630 vs 123,857 characters). Per file the gap was 2.6x to 27x. The crawl's wall time of 1,709 s matches the RUN.jsonl crawl_start and crawl_end timestamps. The licence caveat is right: pymupdf is the optional `ocr` extra (pyproject.toml:33) and is AGPL-3.0. pypdfium2 5.13.0 is already importable in this interpreter, which makes the permissive benchmark cheap to run. Switching changes extracted text, and so text_chars, grounding and golden results, across the corpus. That needs a re-parse into a copy, a diff and a recorded decision, so it is not auto-fixable.

rebuild_corpus.sh:20 runs a full `parse --ocr`, and cli.parse (cli.py:325 onwards) calls build_parsed_doc for every raw/**/fetch_meta.json with no skip. The double parse happens only when OUT is a fresh directory. The script's default OUT is ./data/corpus, the live corpus (line 5). In that default in-place run, the crawl skips unchanged documents (crawler.py:263-269, `skipped_duplicate`) and the legacy import skips unchanged records (cli.py:727-730, `store.is_unchanged`). Step 4 is then the only step that re-parses held documents with the current parser, which is how a D-024-style parser change reaches the corpus. The proposed `--only-status ocr_needed` would silently drop that re-parse in the default invocation. Also, crawler._collect never loads OCR sidecars, so on a fresh OUT step 4 also performs the OCR, not only sidecar re-attachment. The waste is real but occurs once per from-scratch rebuild, a rare operation, so Backlog. The correct fix needs a PARSER_VERSION stamp (`--changed-only`) or an explicit fresh-OUT branch in the script, so M and not auto-fixable.

The code is as claimed. scrape.py:84 calls `self.fetcher.fetch(url)` without etag or last_modified. Page (scrape.py:30-37) carries no headers. store_artifact (download.py:79-84) detects 'unchanged' only after the full body has been downloaded and hashed. _download_and_seed (harvest.py:424-432) then calls _seed, and seed_one runs parse_artifact (seed.py:49) before upsert_record reports 'skipped' (seed.py:76-77). The impact is overstated, though. The catalogue (read-only) holds exactly 1 record (govza_dismissal_code_2025, statute, ocr_needed). The only live-capable source is behind five operator gates (D-019), and ccma_official_publications is disabled because robots returns 403 (D-021, ccma_sources.yaml:29-51). Today the waste is one 1.96 MB request plus one 16-page parse per manually gated harvest, which is negligible. 'Grows linearly' depends on sources that are currently blocked. This is a real deviation from resume-by-validator, but Backlog rather than Next Sprint.

The hook exists: parse_artifact(..., stored_text=...) at ccma/extract.py:196-214, with pipeline.save_ocr_text/load_ocr_text (pipeline.py:132-155) and parse.ocr.ocr_pdf (parse/ocr.py:153). The catalogue confirms GG 53294 is the only record and is ocr_needed. However, (1) the item is already in dead-code.md ("CCMA engine has no OCR step ... Reuse parse/ocr.ocr_pdf and a raw/.../ocr.txt sidecar in ccma seed"), so the only new evidence is the existing stored_text parameter. (2) The helpers cannot be reused exactly as they are: the stored_text branch hard-codes the provenance note "text reused from the main corpus text/ store" (extract.py:213), which would mislabel a machine OCR transcription. It also skips the substantive_chars check and sets no capped confidence, so parse_artifact needs a separate note/confidence argument. (3) As a cost finding the waste is hypothetical: the engine has no OCR step today, so nothing is being repeated. This is a feature gap with a sound design note: Backlog, M, already recorded.

critic.dimension: Completeness critic: gaps none of the seven reviewers raised
critic.summary: The seven reviews missed the legal-output layers: the navigator's deadline logic, the tagger's outcome labels and the CCMA knowledge layer's "holdings". All three produce wrong statements on real data. With a conciliation certificate on file, the navigator still says the referral is late and tells the employee to apply for condonation, and it gives no deadline for requesting arbitration (LRA s136(1)(b), whose wording is in 2 of 3 held LRA copies). Of the 6 judgments carrying a non-review outcome label, 4 are wrong, and 2 say the opposite of the court's order. If the 12 held judgments were seeded through local_corpus, find_holding would turn 6 of them into "The decision-maker found" quotes at high confidence, and none would be the court's own complete finding. findings.title: Navigator tells an employee holding a conciliation certificate to apply for condonation, and gives no arbitration-request deadline
findings.evidence: late = any(d.status is DeadlineStatus.EXPIRED for d in deadlines[:1])
findings.what: When certificate_date is set (conciliation already happened), the first deadline is still the 30-day conciliation referral, computed from the dismissal date. It is almost always EXPIRED by then, so `late` is True. The route then adds 'Apply for condonation of the late referral' (lra_191_2), the checklist adds 'Condonation or late-referral issue', and render.py prints 'PASSED - condonation needed'. On the arbitration track (conduct, capacity, unknown, constructive and ULP cases) no post-certificate deadline exists at all, although LRA s136(1)(b) requires the arbitration request within 90 days of the certificate. The golden case retrenchment-certificate-issued encodes the 'expired' status.
findings.why: Deadlines are the navigator's main value (D-022). A certificate proves the referral was accepted, so telling that employee to seek condonation is a false legal statement. Most dismissal disputes go to arbitration, and that track's next real deadline after conciliation is missing.
findings.how: In Navigator._deadlines, when certificate_date is set, mark the conciliation step as done (a new DeadlineStatus such as COMPLETED, or omit it) and compute `late` only from deadlines still pending. For Track.ARBITRATION and ELECTION, add 'Request arbitration' due add_days(certificate_date, 90), grounded on a new Provision lra_136_1_b. Its quote is the held wording 'within 90 days after the date on which that certificate was issued'. Update the two affected golden cases and send them for the pending lawyer review.
findings.expected_impact: Removes a false condonation instruction from every assessment that has a certificate (golden cases retrenchment-certificate-issued and automatically-unfair-protected-strike-late-at-labour-court today). Adds the missing deadline for the arbitration track; the wording already grounds in 2 of 3 held LRA copies.
findings.proving_test: Navigator(...).assess(CaseFacts(reason='conduct', event_date=2026-06-01, certificate_date=2026-08-01), 2026-10-07): no route step with basis lra_191_2, no condonation checklist item, and a deadline due 2026-10-30 with basis lra_136_1_b.

findings.title: Judgment outcome labels come from the first matching phrase anywhere in the text; 4 of 6 non-review labels are wrong, 2 inverted
findings.what: _infer_outcome returns the first category whose phrase appears anywhere in the document, in priority order: a passing mention, a party's claim, a quoted commissioner finding or a general proposition. The code comment says 'Anything ambiguous stays unknown' and 'a wrong outcome label is worse than an absent one'. The held judgments contradict that. [2014] ZALCD 70 is labelled unfair_substantive, but its order substitutes 'dismissal was substantively fair'. [2011] ZALCCT 10 is labelled automatically_unfair, but its order is that the employee 'was not dismissed'. [2000] ZALAC 4 is labelled automatically_unfair from one s187(1)(e) mention, yet the appeal was upheld and the case concerns a prospective employee. [2014] ZALAC 49 is labelled unfair_procedural from a general PAJA proposition. The remedy labels share the flaw: ZALAC 31 is labelled 'compensation' because the employee 'sought compensation'.
findings.why: documents.outcome, the parsed JSON and the CCMA engine (extract.py:232 into case cards, scenario outcome_range_observed and contra_records) all carry these labels. A RAG layer or reader would be told that a court found the opposite of what it ordered. That breaks the never-invent guarantee in the same way as D-006, D-011 and D-016. None of the seven reviews looked at label accuracy; pipeline.py:392 covered only labels stored on statutes.
findings.how: Infer the outcome only from the decisive part of the text: after the last 'Order', 'ORDER', 'Award' or 'In the premise' heading, or the final ~15% when there is none. Ignore matches preceded by words of report or claim (claimed, contends, submitted, commissioner found, whether). Return UNKNOWN when the categories found conflict. Apply the same section restriction to _infer_remedy. Re-parse afterwards and diff the outcome column.
findings.expected_impact: Removes 4 wrong outcome labels and 1 wrong remedy label out of 7 labelled judgments, with every future crawled judgment protected the same way. Expected effect: more 'unknown' labels and no inverted ones.
findings.proving_test: Unit: a text whose narrative says the commissioner 'found the dismissal ... substantively unfair' and whose ORDER says 'dismissal was substantively fair' gives Outcome.FAIR or UNKNOWN, never UNFAIR_SUBSTANTIVE. Real-corpus test (skipped if absent): the 4 citations above no longer carry their current labels.

findings.title: CCMA case cards present party claims and mid-sentence fragments as 'The decision-maker found', at high confidence
findings.what: find_holding takes the last _FINDING_RE match anywhere, including claims, quoted cases and footnotes. It starts the quote at the previous newline, which is mid-sentence in hard-wrapped PDF/SAFLII text. The paragraph locator comes from ParagraphMap, which accepts '[2007]'. On the 12 held judgments, 6 yield a holding. ZALAC 31 gives 'development as a dismissal, which he claimed was unfair...', the employee's claim. ZALCCT 10 gives a quote of another case. ZALAC 49 and ZALCJHB 364 give general propositions. ZALC 98 and ZALCD 70 give fragments starting mid-sentence. Two carry locators 'para 2007' and 'para 2009'. build_record_units marks each 'confidence: high', writes the strategy note 'The decision-maker found: "..."', and harvest.py audits it as 'unit quotes a published finding verbatim'. The only test uses a one-line fictional finding.
findings.why: D-020 permits high confidence only for a verbatim quoted finding. These are verbatim but not findings, so a reader cannot detect the error, which is the failure D-020 exists to prevent. The catalogue holds 0 knowledge units today, so this triggers on the first `ccma harvest -s local_corpus --popia-ack`.
findings.how: Only accept matches inside the decision section (after an Order/Award heading, or the last paragraph block). Reject sentences containing claim or report verbs (claimed, contends, submitted, alleged, 'the commissioner found'). Find the sentence start with _SENTENCE_END_RE over whitespace-normalised text rather than the line start. Drop the paragraph locator when it is year-shaped. Otherwise return None, so the card falls back to 'medium'. Apply the same section restriction to the _FAIR_FINDING_RE fallback in extract.py:233, which also matches issue statements such as 'whether the dismissal of the applicant was ... fair'.
findings.expected_impact: Prevents up to 6 false high-confidence 'findings' from the current corpus, and the same pattern on every future award or judgment.
findings.proving_test: Unit: find_holding('He regarded this\ndevelopment as a dismissal, which he claimed was unfair.') is None. A wrapped order sentence returns the whole sentence. The locator is never a 4-digit year. Real-corpus test (skipped if absent): no holding for ZALAC 31 or ZALCCT 10.

findings.title: Navigator accepts final-decision and certificate dates after the assessment date, so a year typo turns an 18-day deadline into 383 days
findings.evidence:
if facts.event_date > as_of:
            raise ValueError("event_date is after the assessment date")
findings.what: Only event_date is checked against as_of. final_decision_date, certificate_date and became_aware_date may be in the future, and CaseFacts only checks them against event_date. Measured: dismissal 2026-08-01 with the appeal outcome typed 2027-09-25 instead of 2026-09-25 gives 'Refer ... for conciliation' due 2027-10-25, 383 days left, status open. The true deadline was 2026-10-25. A certificate dated 2027-01-05 is also accepted. The interview's TerminalAsker.when accepts any ISO date.
findings.why: Deadlines are calendar days, never extended, and 'a late filing costs far more than an early one' (D-022). A typo should be refused (exit 2), not turned into an 'open' deadline more than a year away.
findings.how: In Navigator.assess, raise ValueError when any of final_decision_date, became_aware_date or certificate_date is after as_of. The CLI and MCP already map ValueError to exit 2 or 'invalid facts'. Optionally, have TerminalAsker re-ask for a future date.
findings.expected_impact: Removes a silent path to a wildly wrong deadline; costs one comparison per field.
findings.proving_test: Navigator().assess(CaseFacts(reason='conduct', event_date=2026-08-01, final_decision_date=2027-09-25), date(2026,10,7)) raises ValueError. `navigate assess` with those facts exits 2.

findings.title: Neutral citations and wrapped years are read as paragraph markers: 27% of judgment tag locators are years
findings.what: _PARA_MARKER_RE accepts any 1-4 digit bracketed number at a line start. SAFLII text puts the neutral citation '[1998] ZALAC 13' on its own line (breadcrumbs and cited authorities), and hard-wrapped text produces lines like '1995. He'. Across the 12 held judgments, 114 marker matches are year-shaped (106 bracket, 8 plain), and 103 of the 386 paragraph references stored in tags are years such as '1952', '1998' and '2014'.
findings.why: D-005 says being able to point at the paragraph is the point of rule-based tags. A locator of 'para 2014' points at nothing, and it flows into CCMA key_paragraphs and holding locators ('para 2007').
findings.how: Add a negative lookahead after the bracket form for a court code or law-report series, e.g. (?!\s*(?:ZA[A-Z]{2,8}|\(?[A-Z]{2,}\)?)\b). Reject plain-form labels between 1900 and 2099. Optionally require the markers to be roughly increasing.
findings.expected_impact: Removes about 103 of 386 (27%) bogus paragraph locators on judgments after re-parse; protects the CCMA knowledge-card locators.

findings.title: `navigate assess` exits 0 ('grounded') when no corpus exists and every provision is not_checked
findings.what: _run escalates only NOT_FOUND. With --out pointing at a directory with no corpus, corpus_source returns None, all 21 provisions are not_checked, and the command exits 0. Measured on a non-existent scratch path, the result was exit 0. The default --out is the relative 'data/corpus', which does not exist when run from the project root 'SA Labour LAW'. `navigate provisions` treats the same state as exit 3 (tests/test_navigator.py:464-465), and no test covers assess without a corpus.
findings.why: The documented contract is 'exit 0 grounded, 3 wording not found'. A script, or an advice-office wrapper running from the wrong directory, gets a success code for output in which nothing was checked. Only a Markdown warning signals it.
findings.how: In _run, also raise typer.Exit(3), or a distinct code 4, when Grounding.NOT_CHECKED is in grounding_summary. Print to stderr that no corpus was found at --out. Add a CLI test.
findings.expected_impact: Makes ungrounded output detectable by exit code, consistent with `navigate provisions`; a two-line change.
findings.proving_test: runner.invoke(app, ['navigate','assess', f, '--out', str(tmp_path/'none'), '--as-of','2026-10-07']).exit_code == 3 (or 4), and the output names the missing corpus.

findings.title: Acceptance criterion 5 ('unchanged bodies are not re-downloaded') cannot fail; it passes while 89.6 MB was re-downloaded
findings.what: The check sums bytes only over events that are already 304 or cached, so `transferred` is 0 by construction. A 200 re-download of unchanged bytes is never counted. In the current RUN.jsonl, 24 fetches returned 304 with 0 bytes, so the criterion prints PASS. The same log shows 18 URLs (17 of them held documents, e.g. a 24.5 MB MIBCO gazette) fetched 200 twice with identical sizes about 2 minutes apart: 89,572,052 repeat bytes. The Cost reviewer found the causes (http.py:320, crawler.py:258), but the gate that should catch them is vacuous.
findings.why: The tool's own docstring says it 'checks evidence, not intent'. A gate that cannot fail certifies the resume guarantee (architecture.md: '0 bytes') while it is being violated, and it will not catch a regression after the ETag fix.
findings.how: In criterion 5, also group stage=='fetch' events with status 200 by URL. Fail when the same URL has more than one 200 with equal byte counts, or when a 200 body's sha256 equals the fetch_log or documents.content_sha256 already held for that URL. Report the repeat bytes as evidence.
findings.expected_impact: Criterion 5 flips to FAIL on today's corpus (17 documents, 89.6 MB of repeats), then guards the Cost fixes against regression.
findings.proving_test: A synthetic RUN.jsonl with one URL fetched 200 twice at equal bytes, plus one 304, gives criterion 5 = FAIL and evidence naming the repeat bytes. The existing all-304 case still passes.
